content: Isoniazid-resistant tuberculosis (Hr-TB) cases can present with or without mutations in the katG gene, and treatment may involve either standard-dose or high-dose isoniazid. Similarly, Hr-TB cases may or may not involve mutations in the inhA promoter region, with treatment again potentially involving normal or high doses of isoniazid. In some patients, additional agents such as ethambutol, pyrazinamide, or injectable drugs may be ineffective. Specific patient populations include those with prior TB treatment, extensive disease, HIV infection (with or without antiretroviral therapy), children aged 0–14 years, and individuals with diabetes. Treatment outcomes of interest include: 1. Completion of therapy or bacteriological cure by the end of treatment. 2. Treatment failure, with or without subsequent relapse. 3. Survival or death during treatment. 4. Adverse reactions to anti-TB medications, categorized by severity, type, and affected organ systems. 5. Development or amplification of drug resistance, particularly to rifampicin. Relapse is defined as the recurrence of disease within two years following successful treatment completion. Studies on Hr-TB treatment were primarily identified from a systematic review conducted in 2016, with data sourced from PubMed and other databases. The review included cohort studies with at least 20 Hr-TB patients or randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The analysis was updated through February 2016, and standardized patient-level data were collected for comparison of treatment regimens. Treatment regimens were grouped based on their primary components (isoniazid [H], rifampicin [R], ethambutol [E], pyrazinamide [Z], fluoroquinolones [FQ], and streptomycin [S]) and duration (6 months or longer). Relapse and treatment failure were combined for analysis, and treatment success was compared against this composite outcome. Mortality was reported in all studies but could not be analyzed as a function of regimen length due to individualized treatment approaches in many cases. The analysis adjusted for covariates such as age, gender, HIV co-infection, AFB smear positivity, chest radiographic cavitation, prior TB treatment history, and resistance to other first-line drugs. Statistical methods accounted for inter-study differences in patient populations and data collection practices. Risk differences were calculated using fixed-effects generalized linear mixed models, and results were summarized in GRADE tables. Key findings include: Six months of treatment with rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide (6REZ) was associated with a slightly higher likelihood of treatment success compared to longer regimens (7–9 months of REZ), though this effect was not statistically significant when a single large study was excluded. Adding isoniazid to the regimen did not show additional benefit. The use of fluoroquinolones (FQ) was associated with higher odds of treatment success when pyrazinamide was administered for less than four months. However, the comparator group also had high success rates, making it unclear if FQ provided additional benefit when pyrazinamide was used for the full duration. FQ use was associated with lower odds of death and reduced acquisition of rifampicin resistance. Regimens including streptomycin (S) did not show improved outcomes, even when pyrazinamide was used for less than four months. The odds of death were lower for patients on S-containing regimens, but this effect was not statistically significant in analyses restricted to studies included for treatment success. In conclusion, six months of REZ appears to achieve high treatment success rates in Hr-TB patients. Adding fluoroquinolones to these regimens may reduce the risk of death and rifampicin resistance acquisition and could increase success rates when pyrazinamide is used for less than four months, potentially mitigating hepatotoxicity risks. However, the use of streptomycin was not associated with improved outcomes. Patients with extensive disease or additional drug resistance may benefit from extended treatment durations or the addition of isoniazid, fluoroquinolones, or streptomycin to the REZ regimen. This analysis was based on data from 5,537 patients across 33 databases, with 5,418 patients included in the final analysis. Only 2% of the patients were children, precluding specific analyses for this subgroup. The study was approved by the Research Ethics Board of the Montreal Chest Institute, McGill University Health Centre, and local ethics boards as necessary.
